analysis.one_liner: Adds years of patent monopoly to one brand-name anti-inflammatory drug, delaying cheaper generics.
analysis.headline: Despite 33 bipartisan cosponsors and a subcommittee hearing, the bill never got a committee or floor vote and died when the 102nd Congress ended in January 1993.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would amend federal patent law to extend the patent on a single product: any drug described as a non-steroidal anti-inflammatory whose maker filed a new drug application in 1982, waited at least 78 months for Food and Drug Administration approval, and was approved in 1988 [S2] [S3]. Those conditions describe one specific drug, not a class, so the extension would go to one patent holder [S2] [S3]. The extra years would come off the patent's current expiration date and equal the time the application sat at the FDA minus 790 days [S3]. While the patent runs, generic versions of the drug cannot be sold, so patients and insurers keep paying the brand-name price [S3].
analysis.who_benefits: The maker of the drug covered by the patent. It would gain additional years of exclusive sales, during which it faces no generic competition and can keep charging brand-name prices [S3].

how_it_helps.text: The bill extends the patent term for a drug meeting narrow conditions: an NSAID whose maker filed a new drug application in 1982, waited at least 78 months for FDA approval, and was approved in 1988 [S2] [S3].

The extension equals the time the drug application was pending before the FDA minus 790 days, added to the patent's current expiration date, and the patentee must notify the Patent and Trademark Office within 90 days of enactment to confirm it [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Patients, insurers, and government health programs that buy the drug. For every extra year of patent life, they would pay the brand-name price instead of the lower price that generic competition brings [S3].
analysis.who_pays_short: Patients and insurers buying the drug

drawbacks.text: The core cost falls on people who need the drug: each added year of patent protection blocks generic versions, keeping prices higher than they would be under competition [S3].

The bill is written so narrowly — a drug filed in 1982, pending at least 78 months, approved in 1988 — that it functions as a private benefit for one patent holder rather than a general patent policy, which is a fair objection to this style of legislation [S2] [S3].

A good-faith case for the bill is real: a patent holder who spends years waiting for FDA approval loses selling time the patent was supposed to guarantee, and the 790-day deduction means the maker would not be made fully whole for that lost time [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's benefit goes entirely to one company — extra monopoly years — while the cost is spread across everyone who buys that drug through higher prices and delayed generics. The fairness argument behind it (FDA delay eats patent life) could be handled by a general, across-the-board rule; instead this bill singles out one product by conditions only it meets [S2] [S3].

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Judiciary Committee, then to its intellectual property subcommittee, which held a hearing on October 31, 1991 — but no subcommittee or committee ever voted it out, and it died when the Congress ended on January 3, 1993 [S5] [S1].

narrative.text: Rep. Rick Boucher (D-VA) introduced the bill on May 8, 1991, joined by 33 cosponsors — 19 Democrats and 14 Republicans [S1] [S4].
It was referred to the House Judiciary Committee the day it was introduced, and on June 7, 1991 sent to the Subcommittee on Intellectual Property and Judicial Administration [S5].
The subcommittee held a hearing on October 31, 1991, but the bill was never reported out of subcommittee or committee and never reached the House floor [S5].
The 102nd Congress ended on January 3, 1993, and the bill died with it [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Consumers and generic drug makers are better off because the bill died: no extra years of monopoly were added, so generics could reach the market sooner and prices could fall. The patent holder lost the chance at extended exclusive sales.

for.what_they_did: Signed on as cosponsors, giving the bill bipartisan support at introduction.

against.name: House Judiciary Committee
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to a subcommittee that held one hearing on October 31, 1991, then never voted it out; the bill never reached the House floor.

sides.party_line_note: Support was bipartisan from the start — 19 of the 33 cosponsors were Democrats and 14 were Republicans [S4] — and no one cast a recorded vote against it, since the bill died in committee without a floor vote [S5].

industries.industry: Brand-name drug maker holding the covered patent
industries.note: The bill would add years of exclusive sales for one drug, during which the maker faces no generic competition and can charge brand-name prices. Its gain is the public's cost, paid at the pharmacy and by insurers.
Every extra patent year is a year generic versions of the drug are kept off the market. Generic makers would have lost the chance to sell a lower-priced copy.
Payers would keep paying brand-name prices during the extended patent term instead of switching to cheaper generics. Ordinary people bear this cost directly.
